en: The *Dhāraṇī of the Destruction of Māra through Immeasurable Gateways*, translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra and Xuanchang during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the Great Forest Multi-storied Hall at Vaiśālī, together with a great [assembly]...
The community of bhikṣus numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought silently to himself:
"My work of transformation is nearing completion; I should now relinquish the life-faculty."
"Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Tathāgata, right there in that place,
commanded the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Go and announce throughout the great trichiliocosm that the assembly of bhikṣus shall gather at once.
Maudgalyāyana replied to the Buddha, "So be it; I shall obey your instructions," and in the space of a single thought-moment, he arrived at the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Proclaiming a great sound that was heard throughout the great trichiliocosm,
forty hundred thousand bhikṣus suddenly gathered at the multi-storied pavilion in the Great Forest.
Upon seeing the World-Honored One, these bhikṣus...
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"I too should now employ my supernormal powers."
He went to where the assembly of bhikṣus in the trichiliocosm resided and addressed everyone there—
those practicing the vehicle of the śrāvakas, those practicing the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and those training in the Mahāyāna.
"All should be gathered at the multi-storied pavilion in the Great Forest.
At that time, Śāriputra, by means of his supernormal powers,
went to the places where the community of bhikṣus throughout the trichiliocosm were residing.
He proclaimed to all those who practice the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and those seeking the Mahāyāna:
"You may now all assemble at the multi-storied pavilion in the Great Forest.
At that time, the great assembly did exactly as he had said.
Having arrived, they prostrated themselves and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas:
"All of you should assemble here immediately."
At that time, there were the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
and the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura.
The Bodhisattva Who Severs All Sorrow and Languor,
the Bodhisattva Who Bestows Upon All Bodhisattvas,
and the Bodhisattva Who Removes All Obstructions.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Gandhahastin Bodhisattva,
and Varapratibhāna Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya and the others arrived together at the place where the Tathāgata was.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed them, saying:
"Sons of good family, you should now go to the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and announce to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas there:
'Whosoever has already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas...'"
And all other bodhisattvas dwelling in non-retrogression,
up to the great bodhisattvas who have reached the stage of being born only once more before attaining buddhahood,
were all caused to assemble.
At that time, the bodhisattvas immediately received the holy decree and traveled throughout the ten directions to summon all the bodhisattvas.
Having heard this proclamation, those great beings [assembled].
They all exclaimed, "Excellent! So be it; we respectfully accept.
At that time, ninety trillion hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas had all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Furthermore, there were three hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression,
as well as hundreds of thousands of millions of great bodhisattvas.
Each and every one of them was in his final birth before Buddhahood. All such bodhisattvas,
by means of their supernormal powers, in a single moment of thought—
They all assembled at the multi-storied pavilion in the Great Forest.
At that time, the great assembly, having seen the World-Honored One,
prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, having seen that the bodhisattvas from the ten directions had all assembled,
Śāriputra immediately thought to himself: "Now I shall request the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, to explain such a matter as this."
By means of my inquiry,
may all doubts of the bodhisattvas be severed, and may they attain profound wisdom and eloquence;
having heard the sublime Dharma from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [may they realize it].
Not for even a single thought-moment have they given rise to neglect or forgetfulness,
until they attain unsurpassed bodhi;
such is the case for all bodhisattvas.
All should cultivate these four pure and sublime practices. What are the four?
The first is the purity of sentient beings.
Second is the purity of the Dharma;
third is the purity of eloquence;
fourth is the purity of the buddha-field.
Furthermore, he causes the bodhisattvas to give rise to the four right mindfulnesses. What are these four?
Right mindfulness of the body, and right mindfulness of speech.
Maintaining right mindfulness within the mind and right mindfulness regarding birth;
furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one gradually attains deep entry into the gate of dhāraṇī.
What are the four? First, attaining the dharani-door of skillful entry for the inexhaustible proclamation of the Dharma.
Second, knowing the faculties of sentient beings and skillfully attaining entry into the dharani-door.
Third, by skillfully knowing the karmic retribution of conditioned phenomena, one also gains entry into the gate of dhāraṇī.
Fourth, by attaining the profound patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), one swiftly and skillfully enters the gate of dhāraṇī.
Then Śāriputra, according to his thoughts, addressed the Buddha, saying: "These bodhisattvas wish to cultivate pure conduct.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on them and explain it for them, so that they may attain its practice."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"These practitioners have resolved upon the vast mind;
if they wish to cultivate the Dharma of a bodhisattva,"
Furthermore, those practitioners who wish to have a mind that is unattached to phenomena, neither grasping nor rejecting them,
should receive, uphold, recite, and keep in mind such wondrous phrases of this dhāraṇī mantra.

1. Āne (ā-ne, with the second syllable pronounced as *nu* and the third as *shi*); 2. Ākṣe (ā-qi, with the second syllable pronounced as *qian* and *zhi*); 3. Mākṣe; 4. Samantamukhe (san-man-duo, with the final syllable pronounced as *mu* and *qi*);
5. Yudhite (yu-di-tu, with the final syllable pronounced as *du* and *quan*); 6. Nirlte; 7. Nirlte (with the final syllable pronounced as *du* and *shi*); 8.

Svāhā (si-pi, with the final syllable pronounced as *pu* and *yi*); 9. Hīlī (xi-xu-qi, with the initial syllable pronounced as *xu* and *qi*); 10. Kāpi (jie-pi, with the final syllable pronounced as *fu* and *mi*); 11. Kā... (jie).

Rohiṇī (52), Vipulācalā (53), Samantamukhī (54), Sarvadhāraṇī (55), Anantāśī (56), Dhāraṇī-dhāraṇī (57), Nidānakula (58).
*Tadyathā* svāhā. (58) At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"The dhāraṇī-mantra which I have just spoken, these bodhisattvas and practitioners [should receive it]."
All should receive, uphold, read, recite, and master [this teaching],
yet they should not grasp at the conditioned or the unconditioned;
they should be undefiled and unattached toward all phenomena.
Nor should one disparage them with a mind of revulsion,
nor should one grasp at them by striving to cultivate them.
This applies whether one takes up conditioned or unconditioned phenomena.
One should quickly distance oneself from them and not cling to them;
one does not perceive the conjunction of phenomena, nor does one perceive their dispersal.
One does not see the arising of phenomena, nor does one see the cessation of phenomena;
nor does one see phenomena coming or going.
Now, one does not see phenomena increasing, nor does one see phenomena decreasing.
One does not perceive the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination,
nor does one perceive the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
One neither proclaims the teaching of the Dharma, nor does one fail to proclaim it.
A bodhisattva should always maintain right mindfulness:
the Buddhas are neither form nor formless;
they are neither with marks nor without marks.
Neither unrighteous nor not unrighteous;
neither non-precept nor not non-precept;
neither concentration nor non-concentration.
Neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom;
neither liberation nor lack of liberation;
neither the knowledge and vision of liberation nor lack of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Neither of noble lineage nor not of noble lineage;
neither with retinue nor without retinue;
neither practicing nor not practicing.
Neither arrived nor not arrived;
neither time nor non-time;
neither the aggregates, bases, and elements, nor not the aggregates, bases, and elements.
Neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom;
neither preaching the Dharma nor not preaching the Dharma;
neither purity through self nor purity through another.
It is neither the purity of sentient beings nor their impurity;
it is neither for one's own benefit nor for the benefit of others;
it is neither the Dharma nor the Vinaya.
It is neither purity of body and speech nor purity of mind;
furthermore, it is not the purity of conduct in the past, future, or present.
It is for neither oneself nor for others.
I tell you, Śāriputra:
speaking in this manner is what is called a bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the Buddha;
it fully encompasses and includes all dharmas.
It is named "The Subtle Dhāraṇī of the Universal Collection of All Dharmas, Reaching Forever [to Their Source].
It is also named "The Gate of the Dhāraṇī of Supreme Unimpeded Eloquence of the Ultimate Truth."
It is also called the Dharani-door that Fulfills All Vows;
it is also called the Dharani-door of the Profound Samadhis that Necessarily Attain a Portion of Bodhi.

It is also called the "Dhāraṇī Door of Discerning and Encompassing All Other Roots of Goodness," and it is also called the "Dhāraṇī Door of the True Practice of the Sublime Meaning of the Nature and Characteristics of the Dharma-Treasury."
It is also called the "Dhāraṇī Door of the Expedient Means of the Conditioned that Surpasses and Subdues All Māras.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, this dhāraṇī is called the "Exposition of Immeasurable Dharma Doors."
All these practitioners shall obtain this profound benefit and meaning, and swiftly attain the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
Why is this so? Because this is a dhāraṇī.
It is called the profound Dharma-treasury of all merits of the Mahāyāna definitively realized by all Buddhas.
This place is named the Dharani-gate of the undefiled Dharma-precepts that shatter the cycle of birth and death for all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Seeking nothing within empty dharmas, Not engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding bodhi,
One accords with the nature of the dharma-realm And swiftly attains dhāraṇī.
Diligently listen to and study this sutra;
therein you shall achieve the accomplishment of the inexhaustible dhāraṇī.
If one desires to seek the wisdom of omniscience and bodhi, one should uphold this dhāraṇī.
Because this practitioner attains the cultivation of *dhāraṇī*,
they hear the Buddhas of the ten directions extensively expounding all realms of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Having heard all these teachings, they profoundly understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Just as the radiance of the sun shines forth, so too is their clear understanding;
by attaining the cultivation of the most supreme and subtle dhāraṇī,
and through upholding this sūtra, they shall constantly behold all Buddhas.
Even if all sentient beings were to pose difficult questions for the duration of an entire eon,
the practitioner would be able to resolve them all;
such is the eloquence of awakening that it can never be exhausted.
Such practitioners as these are indeed the sons of the Dharma;
having already drawn near to the supreme and unsurpassed path of the bodhisattvas,
those who delight in hearing this sutra shall draw near to such a Dharma teacher.
These Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not merely keep the practitioner in mind,
but also take pity on all sentient beings, just as a compassionate mother loves her child;
such a person, while walking through the world, upholds this dhāraṇī.
At that time, one will be able to see ten million World-Honored Ones.
If a person has committed various sins over a thousand million kalpas in previous lives,
by upholding this sutra for a single month, all those sins will be completely extinguished.
All the World-Honored Ones shall extend their hands to him;
even if bodhisattvas were to accumulate merit for a hundred million eons,
if they can maintain this dhāraṇī for a single month, [their merit would be equal].
The retribution of merit thus obtained— its blessings surpass those of all sentient beings within the three realms; even if they were all to become Māras,
none could obstruct or destroy this one who upholds the dhāraṇī.
If a practitioner recollects this supreme dhāraṇī and is further able to constantly recite and maintain it, until the attainment of bodhi—
this exposition of the dhāraṇī is called "Definitive Retention."
All sentient beings shall, at that very place,
manifest before them and attain the path of unsurpassed bodhi upon hearing this dhāraṇī spoken by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
In an instant, one shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
if one delights in these Buddhas and wishes to know their locations,
one should practice and uphold this sutra, and all shall be fulfilled according to one's intent.
If one desires to attain a pure and most wondrous Buddha-field,
with a radiance that is exceedingly clear and penetrating, and to be fully endowed with a multitude of śrāvakas—
one should uphold this dhāraṇī; then all shall surely obtain it.
The practitioner should apply themselves with diligence; for seven days and seven nights, they should contemplate the dhāraṇī.
They should behold eight billion buddhas and not think of evil thoughts, nor should they entertain any other thoughts.
Dedicate your thoughts solely to such a sutra; you will swiftly attain dhāraṇī.
Just as one who has entered the great ocean seeks no other treasure, once this dhāraṇī is attained, one will never again desire or take pleasure in anything else.
Therefore, one who refines this sutra desires to draw near to profound bodhi;
they shall attain the unsurpassed path and reach the state of tranquil extinction.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
A bodhisattva practitioner who is endowed with four dharmas attains dhāraṇī.
What are these four? They are:
being unattached to impure desires.
They do not give rise to envy toward sentient beings;
they bestow wealth and goods with a heart free from regret or stinginess;
and day and night they constantly delight in practicing wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas,
they attain dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
Abandon those defiled desires and cast off the base conduct of Māra;
through such causes and conditions of desire, one enters the realm of hell.
Regarding the fame and profit of others' kin, do not give rise to a jealous mind.
With eyes of compassion, one observes sentient beings, who possess great majesty and wondrous forms;
yet when these beings engage in disputes and litigation, it all arises from this body.
Therefore, one should abandon attachment, and one will surely attain dhāraṇī.
Constantly seeking the Dharma day and night, With a single mind delighting in the practice for enlightenment,
One will then be able to attain this *dhāraṇī*; Thus,
one should constantly cultivate these four dharmas before oneself.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed Śāriputra:
"These four dharmas should always be cultivated and studied.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are another four dharmas."
The practitioner who possesses these attains dhāraṇī. What are the four?
First, one should always diligently cultivate the practice of an araṇya.
Second, they are capable of enduring and upholding that profound Dharma-patience.
Third, they do not cling to gain or reputation.
Fourth, they abandon all objects of affection and attachment, relinquishing them entirely.
Even at the cost of their own bodies and lives, let alone other material possessions.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas,
they attain dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Always practice in the araṇya, Abiding in heedfulness and diligently cultivating a mind of profound patience; One should act as if one's head were on fire."
This practice is most supreme, praised by all Buddhas;
one does not give rise to thoughts of greed or attachment toward other retinues, fame, profit, offerings, or any material wealth.
Having few desires and being content, like a bird that makes no store, having already obtained this human body, one should always cultivate all manner of goodness.
How wonderful it is to attain the Buddha-dharma! Leaving the household life, one abandons the root of suffering.
All afflictions such as pride have been completely purified;
one should diligently practice reverence and honor the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Those who crave gain lose mindfulness and wisdom, and they also forfeit their faith, ethical discipline, and the Dharma.
One is very far from awakening; therefore, one should abandon greed.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a practitioner should further accomplish four dharmas.
One attains dhāraṇīs.
What are the four? There are eight characters of meaning.
What are the eight?
They are as follows: the syllable A is the ultimate truth;
all dharmas enter into the meaning of non-self.
*La* refers to the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
These marks and signs have the meaning of entering the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata.
*Va* refers to an infant.
The Dharma of the infant is the definitive entry into the meaning of wisdom.
*Ja* refers to the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
it is the entry of birth, old age, and so forth into the state of non-arising and non-ceasing.
*Ka* refers to the performance of karma;
entering into the state where there is no retribution for karma.
*Dha* refers to the dhāraṇī-dharma of total retention (*saṃdhāraṇa*).
One enters the dharma-realm through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
"Śa" refers to śamatha and vipaśyanā; through śamatha and so forth, one enters into all dharmas.
"Kṣa" means that all phenomena are without abiding and without exhaustion;
they are neither destroyed nor possessed of before or after.
In this way, all phenomena enter into nirvāṇa.
These eight characters all enter into this meaning;
the bodhisattva should follow and enter them.
This is called the first primary dharma.
One should skillfully transcribe and diligently uphold this dhāraṇī scripture;
this is called the practitioner’s entry into the second dharma.
Every half-month, one should recite and contemplate this dhāraṇī-vidyā;
this is called the practitioner’s entry into the third dharma.
The practitioner should always single-mindedly contemplate this dhāraṇī-vidyā.
Causing all sentient beings to be entirely joyful and inducing their minds to strive for diligence and acuity—
this is called the practitioner’s entry into the fourth dharma.
Śāriputra, when a practitioner is fully endowed with these four dharmas,
they attain this dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
Regarding the dhāraṇī for upholding [this teaching]:
those who contemplate these eight characters should, every half-month, diligently and constantly recite them;
in this regard, sentient beings should practice and maintain constant mindfulness.
By drawing near to the vast and profound wisdom of enlightenment,
one will certainly be able to perceive all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
therefore, one should cultivate a mind of diligent study toward this Dharma.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There are four dharmas that bring benefit to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they should always be practiced with single-minded devotion.”
What are the four? First, maintaining right mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Second, ultimately being free from all demonic activities.
Third, such a person will swiftly be freed from karmic obstructions.
Fourth, they will quickly attain uninterrupted, subtle, and profound eloquence.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, these are the four dharmas.
The practitioner should diligently and single-mindedly cultivate this dhāraṇī;
they will certainly obtain the benefits of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
One should maintain right mindfulness of all Buddhas;
All demons shall remain unaware, and one will swiftly distance oneself from them all.
Furthermore, one shall obtain immeasurable billions of dharanis of eloquence, Which eliminate all karmic obstructions.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "In the remote past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Ratnottama-jvālā-prabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
He appeared in the world.
Śāriputra, at the time of the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Ratnavijaya-jvālā-prabha,
there was a wheel-turning king named Jyotiṣprabha.
Possessing the seven treasures, he ruled over the four continents.
That king had a son named Acintyaguṇaviśeṣottama.
When this prince reached the age of one thousand six hundred years, [he went] to the presence of the Buddha Ratnavijaya-jvālāloka.
Upon first hearing this dharani method,
he immediately attained understanding and practiced it with single-minded diligence;
for seventy thousand years, day and night, he did not slacken.
He never grew weary or indolent, nor did he close his eyes for even a moment.
Furthermore, during seventy thousand years,
the prince renounced his body, life, wealth, and royal throne.
Furthermore, for seventy thousand years, he practiced diligently by walking meditation in a solitary place, his side never touching the ground.
Moreover, he did so in the presence of nine billion, one hundred thousand nayutas of Tathāgatas.
Having heard the Dharma being preached, they all received, upheld, read, recited, and mastered it thoroughly.
The prince then left the household life to practice the Way;
after ninety thousand years, he had received, upheld, and perfected such immeasurable dharanī-doors.
When this bhikṣu had accomplished these things,
he extensively proclaimed and demonstrated this meaning for the sake of sentient beings.
The bhikṣu-prince, right in this very life, [attained realization].
He transformed eighty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings,
causing them all to dwell securely in the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and likewise to realize the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, at that time there was among the assembly a son of a householder named Candradhvaja.
This son of a householder [approached] that bhikṣu, the Dharma-preacher.
Having heard these immeasurable dharanī-gates,
he immediately rejoiced in them and received them upon the crown of his head.
By virtue of the causal conditions of this merit from the roots of goodness of such rejoicing, Candradhvaja—
Having encountered ninety billion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
he reverently made offerings to them and attained this supreme dharma of dhāraṇī.
He was the most preeminent among all debaters.
Furthermore, he attained the foremost uninterrupted eloquence as the prince-bhikṣu.
Having made offerings to these Buddhas for three kalpas, he realized the Unsurpassed Way.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, do not give rise to doubt or uncertainty.
The prince who was the bhikṣu Dharma Master at that time is none other than the present Tathāgata Amitāyus.
At that time, it was the Buddha Candradhvaja-pradīpa.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"I and the bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa..."
Having all together heard this dharani method, they immediately gave rise to sympathetic joy.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of these roots of goodness and merit,
they passed through forty hundred thousand kalpas.
Constantly and diligently turning his back on the phenomena of birth and death,
he attained the foremost among dhāraṇīs in the presence of ninety billion Tathāgatas.
Their speech is transcendent and their eloquence is preeminent.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, for this reason,
if a practitioner wishes to swiftly attain the unsurpassed path, [they should practice this].
One should uphold this dharani method; however,
if one is unable to uphold, transcribe, read, or recite it,
one should at least give rise to sympathetic joy.
Why is this? It is because by virtue of these roots of goodness, such a practitioner will certainly attain the stage of non-retrogression and reach the Unsurpassed Way;
how much more so for those who receive, uphold, transcribe, read, and recite it!
As for those who extensively expound this to others,
the merit they obtain can be measured by no sentient being whatsoever, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata.
How much more so for those who contemplate it and explain it extensively for others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Having attained this dhāraṇī, It is named 'The Gate of Immeasurability'."
The Buddhas always protect and keep them in mind, so that Māra finds no opportunity;
their karmic obstructions and the dust of afflictions are all swiftly purified.
Having heard this wondrous scripture, they rejoice and immediately transcribe it.
Those who receive, uphold, constantly read, recite, and extensively expound this for others—
among all sentient beings, their merit cannot be measured.
Wherever such practitioners are born, they shall always behold the Buddhas.
Having attained inconceivable faith and being well-versed in the meaning of the profound sūtras,
such a practitioner will swiftly attain the path to supreme bodhi;
their samādhis and supernatural powers are inexhaustible, and their dhāraṇīs are likewise so.
His physical form is ever complete, and his meritorious rewards constantly succeed one another;
He beholds the Buddhas and hears the Dharma, never for a moment lacking them.
Until he attains Bodhi, may he forever preserve these merits.
I recall that in a past life, having already heard this dhāraṇī and beheld Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I attained unsurpassed bodhi—
just as the former Moon-Banner attained the state of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
The bhikṣu Dharma Master, who excelled in past merits,
now beholds the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, Amitābha. He is my [teacher],
as are the immeasurable bodhisattvas within this Bhadrakalpa.
Having heard this sutra together, they rejoice with a profound heart;
if they delight in swiftly drawing near to the path of unsurpassed bodhi,
and also delight in quickly subduing Māra, and further delight in the adornment of the hundred blessings.
One should diligently apply the mind to total retention (*dhāraṇī*); then, to attain this will not be difficult.

If one were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with precious jewels and bestow them as alms upon all beings, so that they all attained abundance; [this merit would still not equal that of the former].
But one who is able to write this sutra— Their merit shall exceed that [of the former].
Therefore, you should listen with tranquility, With a single mind, never distracted,
Whether copying it down, receiving and upholding it, Or reflecting upon it well.
A bodhisattva of wisdom who [studies] such a profound and wondrous scripture shall swiftly attain enlightenment; it shall not be difficult for them to do so.
He further addressed Śāriputra:
If there is a practitioner who single-mindedly maintains mindfulness of this dhāraṇī,
eight yakṣas dwelling on the Snowy Mountains will protect such a practitioner day and night.
They eliminate all decline and affliction and increase one’s power.

What are these eight? First is Śūra (in the Song language, "Valiant and Strong"); second is Cakrāṅka (Firm and Solid); third is Bahuputra (Many Sons); fourth is Nārāyaṇa (the Great Malla); fifth is Narendrarāja (Lord of Men); sixth is Tuṣitaśoka (Capable of Refuting); seventh is Karāla (Fierce Teeth); and eighth is Subāhu (Beautiful Arms).
He addressed Śāriputra:
"The practitioner should use fine white silk to paint images of these eight spirits."
One should use fresh, vibrant colors and ensure they are perfectly pure;
one must not use the glue derived from sentient beings.
If a practitioner wishes to recite this sutra, [they should proceed as follows].
First, one should bathe and don clean garments,
then single-mindedly supplicate these eight spirits and provide them with various kinds of fragrant and pure food and drink.
One should offer various exquisite blended incenses, scattered flowers,
flower garlands, and pure oil lamps as offerings.
Furthermore, the practitioner should decorate the ground with colorful paintings.
Seated upon a circular pedestal with sovereign ease,
his right knee touches the ground and his hand holds an incense burner;
with single-minded compassion, he contemplates immeasurable sentient beings.
If one recites this dhāraṇī mantra seven times in a low voice,
these eight spirits will immediately manifest their bodies;
among the devas of the desire realm, there are bodhisattvas.
When these eight great beings see this practitioner respectfully reciting such a dhāraṇī,
they will also constantly protect and mind them, augmenting their power. Who are these eight?
The Bodhisattva Multitudinous Light,
the Bodhisattva Wisdom Light,
and the Bodhisattva Sunlight.
He questioned the Bodhisattva Praśnavyākaraṇa,
the Bodhisattva Sarvapraṇidhānaparipūrṇa,
and the Bodhisattva Mahābala.
The Bodhisattva Star King,
the Bodhisattva Wondrous Intention—
these eight bodhisattvas and eight spirits.
It causes this practitioner to cultivate with single-minded devotion,
so that they may obtain the power and benefit of the dhāraṇī-dharma,
and cause all sentient beings to cherish and regard them with affection.
All necessities will be provided according to one's wishes without lack,
and within a radius of one hundred yojanas, no calamities or afflictions shall exist.
A practitioner such as this should cultivate the dhāraṇī.
One should form true aspirations, maintain mindfulness with diligence,
delight in all wholesome dharmas,
and distribute the mind’s vast benefits through generosity, ethical discipline, and other virtues.
One should give according to whatever one has, without any stinginess.
A practitioner who upholds this dhāraṇī should also revere the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
They shall constantly maintain reverence for the Triple Gem and single-mindedly cultivate the profound patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
When the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī, [the assembly rejoiced].
Three thousand Ganges-sands of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas all attained this dharani-gate called "Expounding the Immeasurable," and furthermore,
they realized the stage of non-retrogression.
When he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
there will be sixty *bimbara* of devas and humans who have not yet resolved their minds toward unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Now they have all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
what is the name of this sutra?"
"How should it be upheld?
He replied to Śāriputra,
"This sutra is named the *Dhāraṇī of the Total Retention of Immeasurable Gateways*."
It should be upheld thus.
It is also called the *dhāraṇī* for the total destruction of all Māras; it should be upheld thus.
It is also called the *dhāraṇī* for the Bodhisattva’s partial transcendence of the mind; it should be upheld thus.
It is also called the "Dhāraṇī of the Totality of All-Knowledge Attained by a Single Part. Thus it should be upheld.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas—
The bodhisattvas, humans, devas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and all those in the world,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
rejoiced with exuberant delight; they received and upheld it with reverence upon their heads, and having paid homage, withdrew.
The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī for Destroying Māra through Immeasurable Gateways.
